1170.title: The sunnah as second
1170.hook: the sunnah explains and details the Qur'an
1170.howItsDone: Muslims learn the details of prayer, charity and fasting from the sunnah, by watching parents and teachers pray and by studying the hadith and the fiqh built on them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Qur'an as first source, its verses of law read closely, reasons and all. Your line: the book first.

A group of young men have spent some days with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and now they're about to set off home to their people. The Qur'an gives them the command, in Pickthall's words: "Establish worship." It gives it again and again. What it doesn't give is a step-by-step. When to stand, how to bow, what to say, how many units: the text leaves that out. So before they go, in a report kept in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet tells them how to teach the prayer. Pray as you have seen me praying. Today: the sunnah as second.
screen: `ESTABLISH WORSHIP.` → `BUT HOW?` → `PRAY AS YOU HAVE SEEN ME PRAYING.`

segments.voice: First, what sunnah means here: the Prophet's way, what he said, did and approved, carried in the hadith of the last block. In fiqh it stands second, right after the Qur'an. Second, the book points to it. The Qur'an says Allah sent the reminder down to the Prophet so that he would explain to people what had been sent down to them. And it tells believers, in Pickthall's words, "Obey Allah, and obey the messenger." The second source isn't bolted on from outside; the first source names it. Third, how it explains. Scholars describe the sunnah doing more than one job. It details what the Qur'an gives in brief, like the prayer: pray as you have seen me praying. It shows how a general command is carried out: the Qur'an commands the poor-due, and the sunnah sets out which wealth is due and how much. It confirms what the Qur'an already says. And scholars discuss, and differ over, rulings found in the sunnah that the Qur'an doesn't mention. Fourth, who carries it. Sunni schools receive the sunnah through the reports of the companions, weighed by the methods of the last block. Shia scholars receive it also through the Imams of the Prophet's family, whose words and example they hold to be part of it, weighed through their own collections. Both put the sunnah right after the book. That's why the hadith block came first: the second source rests on knowing which reports are sound.
screen: `THE PROPHET'S WAY, SECOND.` · `THE BOOK NAMES IT.` · `IT DETAILS, SHOWS AND CONFIRMS.` · `SUNNI AND SHIA CHANNELS.`

segments.voice: Picture a prayer you've seen or prayed: standing, then bowing, then the forehead resting on the ground. The Qur'an speaks of bowing and prostrating; the shape of those movements, one after another, comes from people watching the Prophet pray and doing what they saw. Picture them slowly, in order, then come back to your own body, your hands, your breath.
The sunnah as second. The Prophet's way, carried in the hadith, standing after the Qur'an in fiqh and explaining it. Today's word.
Your line: the sunnah explains. The book names it, and it fills the book in. Rest well.

1171.title: Consensus of scholars
1171.hook: agreement of the scholars as a source for Sunni schools
1171.howItsDone: Sunni scholars treat a ruling on which the qualified scholars agreed as settled, while Twelver Shia scholars accept consensus when it reflects the view of the Imam; students learn which rulings are held to be agreed and which are differed over.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sunnah as second, the Prophet's way that the book itself names. Your line: the sunnah explains.

What happens when the people who know a subject best all land in the same place? In Sunni legal thought, that landing place has a name, and it counts as a source of law in its own right, after the Qur'an and the sunnah. Not a vote. Not a poll of the public. The agreement of the community's qualified scholars on a ruling. It sounds simple. Pinning down what it means, whose agreement counts, and how anyone could know it happened, kept scholars arguing. Today: ijma'.
screen: `EVERYONE LANDS IN ONE PLACE.` → `NOT A VOTE.` → `SIMPLE? NOT QUITE.`

segments.voice: Ijma' means agreement, a coming together on one thing. In Sunni legal theory it names the agreement of the qualified scholars of the community, in a given generation, on a ruling. The grounds? Scholars point to a report that the Prophet ﷺ said his community would not agree upon error. It comes in more than one collection, in different wordings, and critics have weighed its chains differently. Tradition says al-Shafi'i also pointed to a verse that warns against following a way other than the believers' way. What does consensus do? Where it exists, it settles a question. Scholars give examples like the obligation of the daily prayers and the fast of Ramadan, or the gathering of the Qur'an into one written copy that was passed on. And they hold that consensus rests on a text; it doesn't float free of the Qur'an and the sunnah. Then the arguments about agreement itself. Whose agreement counts? Only the companions'? The scholars of any generation? Imam Malik gave special weight to the practice of the people of Medina. Can a consensus even be known, once scholars live scattered across many lands? A saying attributed to Ahmad ibn Hanbal warns that someone who claims consensus may be speaking falsely, since people may have differed without his knowing. And Twelver Shia scholars accept consensus as proof when it reveals the view of the Imam, not as a source standing on its own. So agreement is itself a place where scholars disagree, carefully, which shows how much weight they gave it.
screen: `IJMA': A COMING TOGETHER.` · `WILL NOT AGREE UPON ERROR.` · `CONSENSUS RESTS ON A TEXT.` · `WHOSE AGREEMENT COUNTS?`

segments.voice: Take one ruling scholars give as an example of consensus: the fast of Ramadan is obligatory. Picture its reach, people of different schools, lands and languages, who differ on a great deal, all keeping the same month. Hold that picture for a few breaths.
Ijma'. Agreement: in Sunni law, the agreement of the community's qualified scholars on a ruling, a source standing after the Qur'an and the sunnah. Today's word.
Your line: agreement. Not a vote, but the scholars landing in one place. Until tomorrow.

1172.title: Reasoning by analogy
1172.hook: extending a ruling to a new case by a shared reason
1172.howItsDone: In the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools, jurists use analogy to rule on cases no text names, by finding a shared reason with a case a text does name; Ja'fari jurists do not reason by analogy in this way.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ijma', the agreement of the scholars, not a vote. Your line: agreement.

A woman from the tribe of Juhayna comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Her mother had vowed to make the pilgrimage, and died before she could go. May the daughter go for her? In Sahih al-Bukhari, the answer is yes, and the way he answers is the point. He asks her back: if your mother had owed a debt, would you have paid it? Yes, she says. Then pay what is owed to Allah, for Allah has more right to be paid. A case she understood, a debt, carried over to one she didn't, by what the two shared. Today's word is that move.
screen: `A MOTHER'S VOW, UNFULFILLED.` → `WOULD YOU PAY HER DEBT?` → `THEN PAY THIS ONE.`

segments.voice: The word is qiyas, measuring one thing against another. In Sunni legal theory it names a way of reaching a ruling for a new case no text addresses directly, by finding an old case a text does address, and a reason the two share. Its parts: the root, the asl, the original case. The branch, the far', the new case. The 'illa, the shared reason behind the ruling. And the hukm, the ruling itself, which travels from root to branch along that reason. An example the books reach for is wine. The Qur'an names strong drink among the things believers are told to leave aside, in Surah al-Ma'idah, verse ninety. Jurists asked what it is about wine that carries the ruling. Not the grape. Not the color. The intoxication. So when a drink made from something else intoxicates the same way, the ruling reaches it too, by likeness. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says directly that every intoxicant is forbidden, and jurists treat that report as its own text; the wine case is still how the books teach the method. Qiyas isn't a hunch or new law out of nowhere. It starts from a text and travels only as far as the reason travels. If the shared reason is wrong, the analogy fails, and much of the scholars' arguing is over exactly that. Not every school uses it the same way. The Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools count it as a source. Ja'fari jurists, of the Shia, don't reason by analogy in this way; they give reason its own place, and that's tomorrow.
screen: `QIYAS: MEASURING ONE BY ANOTHER.` · `ROOT, BRANCH, REASON, RULING.` · `WINE, AND THE REASON BEHIND IT.` · `THE SCHOOLS DON'T ALL USE IT.`

segments.voice: Take a rule you already keep, like not reading someone's private messages, and name its reason: they're theirs, and weren't opened to you. Then find a new case that shares the reason, a diary left on a table, and see whether the reason travels; if it does, the rule travels with it. If you pray, you can ask for clear sight.
Qiyas. Reasoning by analogy: a ruling carried from an old case to a new one, along the reason they share. Today's word.
Your line: by likeness. A ruling travels only as far as its reason. See you tomorrow.

1173.title: Reason, for Shia jurists
1173.hook: Ja'fari jurists count reason as a source alongside the Qur'an, sunnah and consensus
1173.howItsDone: Ja'fari jurists list the Qur'an, the sunnah, consensus and reason as the sources of law, and Shia Muslims follow the rulings of living jurists trained in this method.

segments.voice: Yesterday: qiyas, a ruling carried from an old case to a new one. Your line: by likeness.

Open al-Kafi, a collection of reports gathered by the scholar al-Kulayni and read closely by Shia Muslims, and the very first section is not about prayer, or fasting, or law. It's called the book of reason and ignorance. Before a single ruling, the collection stops to talk about the mind. The Qur'an itself asks its listeners, in Surah al-Baqarah, whether they have no sense, whether they will not use their reason. For Ja'fari jurists, the Shia school of law named for Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, that question isn't only a rebuke. It's a door into the law. Today's word is reason.
screen: `AL-KAFI OPENS WITH REASON.` → `WILL YOU NOT USE YOUR REASON?` → `A DOOR INTO THE LAW.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is 'aql, the mind, the faculty that understands. Ja'fari legal theory names its sources: the Qur'an, the sunnah, consensus, and 'aql, reason. Sunni schools reason too, of course, mostly through analogy, which was yesterday. The Ja'fari path sets analogy aside and gives reason its own seat at the table. What does reason do there? Not invent rulings out of thin air. Ja'fari jurists use it in a few careful ways. One sounds almost too plain to need saying: when the law requires something, it requires whatever that thing can't be done without. Pilgrimage is a duty for those who are able, so the journey to Mecca becomes part of the duty, though no verse says book the ticket and pack the bag. Reason sees the link, and the jurist follows it. Another is the judgment that some things are good or bad in themselves: justice is good, injustice is wrong, and a mind can see this. Ja'fari theology holds that God does not command injustice, and that reason can recognize justice. From there comes a principle stated as a pair: what reason firmly judges, the law also judges, and the reverse. Jurists argue hard over what counts as a firm judgment of reason, and don't let a passing opinion count as one. So here is the fair picture. Sunni and Ja'fari jurists both use the mind. They differ in where they place it: inside analogy, for the Sunni schools that use it, or beside the texts as a source with its own name. Both are trying to read the same revelation without leaving their minds at the door.
screen: `'AQL: THE MIND THAT UNDERSTANDS.` · `REASON AMONG THE SOURCES.` · `WHAT A DUTY CAN'T BE DONE WITHOUT.` · `JUSTICE, SEEN BY THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Pick something you've committed to, being on time for someone or keeping a promise to call, and ask what it can't be done without: leaving earlier, charging the phone, writing it down. Notice that you never chose those links on their own; the first commitment chose them for you. If you pray, you might ask for a clear mind.
'Aql. Reason, the understanding mind; for Ja'fari jurists, a source of law beside the Qur'an, the sunnah and consensus. Today's word.
Your line: reason as a source. Beside the texts, with its own name. Same time tomorrow.

1174.title: The common good
1174.hook: the aims of the law: protect religion, life, mind, lineage and property
1174.howItsDone: Muslim jurists and teachers often explain rulings by the aims of the law, the protection of religion, life, mind, lineage and property, and the schools differ on how far the common good can be used where no text speaks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'aql, reason, a source of law for Ja'fari jurists. Your line: reason as a source.

Pork is forbidden in the Qur'an. So is meat from an animal that died on its own. Then, in the very same passage of Surah al-Baqarah, comes an exception: whoever is driven by necessity, not wanting it and not going beyond the limit, carries no sin. A person starving in the desert with nothing else to eat is not breaking the law by eating. The rule bends, and the text itself bends it. Why would a law make room against its own prohibition? Because, jurists say, the law has aims, and keeping a person alive is one of them. Today's word is the good those aims protect.
screen: `FORBIDDEN FOOD.` → `UNLESS YOU'RE STARVING.` → `WHY WOULD THE LAW BEND?`

segments.voice: The word is maslahah: benefit, welfare, the good of a thing. Muslim jurists asked a large question with it: what is the law for? The scholar al-Ghazali, in his book on legal theory, al-Mustasfa, gave an answer later writers took up. The law, he wrote, aims to protect five things for people: their religion, their life, their mind, their lineage, and their property. Whatever protects those, he called maslahah; whatever harms them, its opposite. Run the five through some familiar rules. Prayer and fasting guard religion. The law of retaliation for killing guards life. The ban on intoxicants guards the mind. The rules of marriage guard lineage, who belongs to whom. The penalty for theft guards property. Each rule has a job, and the jobs explain the exceptions: that's why the starving person may eat, because a food rule gives way when life itself is at stake. The Qur'an puts the spirit plainly, in Surah al-Baqarah: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you." Later, the Andalusian scholar al-Shatibi, of the Maliki school, built a whole study on these aims, the maqasid. Now the honest part. The schools agree that the law serves people's good. They differ on how far maslahah can go on its own, where no text speaks. The Maliki school is known for using it more freely. Others insist it stay tied to a text, so that nobody's private sense of the common good starts writing law. Even the argument is about protecting the same five things.
screen: `MASLAHAH: THE GOOD OF A THING.` · `FIVE THINGS THE LAW PROTECTS.` · `THE AIMS EXPLAIN THE EXCEPTIONS.` · `HOW FAR CAN IT GO ALONE?`

segments.voice: Choose any rule you live under, religious or not: a speed limit near a school, not leaving a child alone near water, fasting rules that let the sick eat. Trace it to a life it keeps safe, a face if you can, and let the rule look a little less like a fence and a little more like a hand.
Maslahah. Benefit, the common good: what the law's aims protect, religion, life, mind, lineage and property. Today's word.
Your line: the aims of the law. Religion, life, mind, lineage, property. Until next time.

1175.title: Custom and place
1175.hook: local custom counts where it doesn't conflict with the texts
1175.howItsDone: Muslim jurists let sound local custom settle questions the texts leave open, such as what counts as reasonable support or the usual terms of a sale, while setting aside customs that conflict with the Qur'an and sunnah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: maslahah, the good the law's five aims protect. Your line: the aims of the law.

A wife brings a money problem to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, Hind bint Utba says her husband, Abu Sufyan, is tight-fisted. He doesn't give enough for her and the children, she says, unless she takes from his money without his knowing. Is she allowed? His answer gives her no number, no amount, no list. Take what is enough for you and your children, he says, in the way that is reasonable. Reasonable by whose measure? Not a verse's. Not a scholar's. What people around her would recognize as fair. Today's word is that recognized measure.
screen: `A TIGHT-FISTED HUSBAND.` → `HOW MUCH MAY SHE TAKE?` → `WHAT IS REASONABLE.`

segments.voice: The word is 'urf, custom: what a community knows and recognizes as normal. Close beside it stands ma'ruf, the known, the decent, the word the Prophet used to Hind. The Qur'an leans on that word too. In Surah al-Baqarah, a father provides food and clothing for a nursing mother in the reasonable way, and the verse gives no figure. What counts as enough food, decent clothing, a fair gift, is left to the people who live it. Jurists turned this into a maxim: custom is given authority. A Hanafi maxim goes further: what people know by custom counts as if it had been written into the contract. If everyone in a town knows the seller delivers the furniture, the buyer doesn't need it in writing. So a ruling can look different in Cairo and in Kuala Lumpur, not because the texts changed, but because the custom it rests on did: what counts as a home's ordinary furnishings, how a dowry is usually split between now and later, what a day's work means. But there's a hard edge. Custom counts only where it doesn't conflict with the texts. A custom of cheating in the market doesn't become permitted because everyone does it. A custom that takes a woman's inheritance doesn't override the Qur'an's shares. Jurists sort customs into sound and corrupt, and only the sound one gets a vote. So 'urf isn't a door for anything at all. It's the space the texts leave open on purpose, for people to fill with what they recognize as decent.

1176.title: The five rulings
1176.howItsDone: Muslim jurists, Sunni and Shia, sort acts into obligatory, recommended, permitted, disliked and forbidden, and books of practical rulings label each act with one of these.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'urf, custom, which counts where it doesn't conflict with the texts. Your line: custom counts.

A small stick of wood, frayed at one end, used to clean the teeth: the siwak. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that if it would not be too hard on his community, he would have ordered them to use it at every prayer. And he held back from making it a command. Between a command and nothing at all, there's a whole range, and that one sentence sits right in the middle of it. Today: what all the sources produce.
screen: `A STICK FOR THE TEETH.` → `NOT A COMMAND, ON PURPOSE.` → `WHAT THE SOURCES PRODUCE.`

segments.voice: The word is ahkam, rulings, the plural of hukm. Jurists sort every human act into five kinds. First, obligatory: the prescribed prayers, the fast of Ramadan. Doing it brings reward; leaving it brings blame. Second, recommended: the siwak, extra prayers, smiling at someone. Doing it brings reward, but leaving it brings no blame. That's where the Prophet placed the siwak, out of mercy. Third, permitted: eating an apple, taking a walk, choosing blue over green. No reward, no blame, just life. Fourth, disliked: wasting water while washing for prayer is an example jurists give. Leaving it brings reward, but doing it brings no sin. Fifth, forbidden: theft, lying to cheat someone. Doing it brings blame. The scale turns religion from a switch, allowed or not, into a dial. A person who keeps the obligatory and avoids the forbidden is inside the law. The recommended is an invitation to go further, and the disliked a gentle warning, not a wall. Sunni and Shia jurists both use these five. In Ja'fari books the names are wajib, mustahabb, mubah, makruh, haram. Sunni books use the same, with some synonyms, like fard for obligatory and mandub for recommended. The Hanafi school draws finer lines: it separates fard from wajib by how certain the evidence is, and splits the disliked into a lighter kind and a heavier one. This week traced where rulings come from: the sunnah, agreement, likeness, reason, the common good, custom. The five are what they produce, and the siwak shows the spirit: the one who brought the law held back from a duty, because a duty is heavy.
